entity.name: Hans Christian Andersen
entity.description: The shoemaker's son who invented the modern fairy tale. Andersen wrote 156 stories — including The Little Mermaid, The Ugly Duckling, and The Emperor's New Clothes — translated into more than 125 languages. He traveled compulsively across Europe and once overstayed his welcome at Charles Dickens' house by four weeks.

story.name: Hans Christian Andersen
story.description: A washerwoman's son leaves Odense at fourteen, fails as an actor in Copenhagen, publishes fairy tales that Danish critics despise, and becomes the most translated Danish author in history.

moments.name: Hans Christian Andersen Is Born to a Shoemaker and a Washerwoman in Odense
moments.subtitle: The boy who will invent the modern fairy tale grows up in poverty
moments.description: On 2 April 1805, Hans Christian Andersen was born in Odense, Denmark, the son of a shoemaker and an illiterate washerwoman. Andersen's father introduced him to literature by reading Arabian Nights aloud, sparking an imagination that would eventually produce 156 fairy tales. When his father died in 1816, eleven-year-old Andersen was sent to a school for poor children and apprenticed first to a weaver, then a tailor. Speculation has persisted that Andersen was actually the illegitimate son of King Christian VIII, though this remains unproven. At fourteen, Andersen left Odense for Copenhagen with little money and no connections, determined to become an actor.

moments.name: Fourteen-Year-Old Andersen Arrives in Copenhagen to Become an Actor
moments.subtitle: A gangly teenager with a soprano voice talks his way into the Royal Danish Theatre
moments.description: In 1819, fourteen-year-old Hans Christian Andersen arrived in Copenhagen with almost no money, seeking employment as an actor. His good soprano voice won him acceptance into the Royal Danish Theatre, but his voice soon changed, ending his singing career. A colleague at the theatre told Andersen he was really a poet, and Andersen took the suggestion to heart, shifting his focus to writing. Jonas Collin, director of the Royal Danish Theatre, took an interest in the awkward young man and persuaded King Frederick VI to pay for Andersen's grammar school education. Andersen later said his school years were the most bitter of his life — a teacher abused him and discouraged him from writing. Copenhagen remained his home base for the rest of his life.

moments.name: Andersen Publishes His First Fairy Tales to Hostile Danish Reviews
moments.subtitle: Critics say fairy tales should educate, not entertain — Andersen disagrees
moments.description: On 8 May 1835, Hans Christian Andersen published his first collection of fairy tales in Copenhagen, a sixty-one-page booklet containing The Tinderbox, Little Claus and Big Claus, The Princess and the Pea, and Little Ida's Flowers. Publisher C.A. Reitzel paid Andersen thirty rigsdalers for the manuscript. Two more installments followed through April 1837, adding Thumbelina, The Little Mermaid, and The Emperor's New Clothes. Danish critics were hostile, calling the informal style immoral and unsuitable for children's literature. Andersen was so discouraged that he waited a full year before publishing the third installment. The nine tales would eventually be translated into more than 125 languages.

moments.name: Andersen Overstays His Welcome at Charles Dickens' Home by Four Weeks
moments.subtitle: A brief visit stretches to five weeks and destroys a literary friendship forever
moments.description: In June 1857, Hans Christian Andersen visited Charles Dickens at his home, Gad's Hill Place in Kent, England. What was planned as a brief stay stretched into five agonizing weeks, much to the distress of Dickens' entire family. Andersen was finally told to leave, and after his departure, Dickens gradually cut off all correspondence. Andersen, who had enjoyed the visit immensely, never understood why his letters went unanswered. The two authors had first met in 1847 at a London party hosted by the Countess of Blessington, where Andersen gushed in his diary about meeting the English writer he loved most. It has been argued that Dickens modeled the obsequious Uriah Heep partly on Andersen's mannerisms.
moments.address: Gad's Hill Place, Higham, Kent, England

moments.name: Hans Christian Andersen Dies in Copenhagen at Seventy
moments.subtitle: Denmark's most famous author passes away after years of declining health
moments.description: On 4 August 1875, Hans Christian Andersen died in Copenhagen at the age of seventy. In his final years, Andersen had suffered from liver cancer and a series of falls. He had been living as a guest in the homes of wealthy friends, a pattern that characterized much of his adult life. Despite being celebrated across Europe — his stories had been translated into dozens of languages and inspired ballets and theatrical adaptations — Andersen remained deeply insecure about his work and his place in Danish literary culture. His 156 fairy tales, including The Ugly Duckling, The Snow Queen, and The Little Match Girl, have since become foundational texts of Western children's literature, read in more than 125 languages worldwide.
